about: The Security screen's checks (docs/security-plan.md): id, group, title, why it matters and advice a person acts on themselves. Rackoon never changes the server. Each core's rules emit findings with these ids (plus ':<item>' for one finding per port or container); spec/scenarios/security-checks.json says which severity each fixture gives.

checks.advice: Nothing to do if this server is reached another way (for example Tailscale SSH or a console).
checks.title: SSH server
checks.why: Every other SSH check reads the OpenSSH server's settings.

checks.advice: Set PermitRootLogin to no (or prohibit-password) in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ and reload ssh.
checks.title: Root login with a password
checks.why: A root password that can be guessed over SSH gives away the whole server.

checks.advice: Once your key logins work, set PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no, then reload ssh.
checks.title: Password logins
checks.why: Passwords can be guessed by bots that scan for SSH all day; keys cannot.

checks.advice: Set PermitEmptyPasswords no (the default) and give every account a password or lock it.
checks.title: Empty passwords
checks.why: An account without a password could log in with nothing at all.

checks.advice: Leave MaxAuthTries at 6 or lower.
checks.title: Login attempts per connection
checks.why: More attempts per connection make guessing cheaper.

checks.advice: Set X11Forwarding no unless you run graphical programs over SSH.
checks.title: X11 forwarding
checks.why: Forwarding graphical programs is rarely needed on a server and widens what a login can reach.

checks.advice: Review the ssh rules in your tailnet policy file; the sshd checks here cover only logins that reach sshd.
checks.title: Tailscale SSH
checks.why: Logins over Tailscale SSH follow your tailnet's SSH policy, not sshd's settings.

checks.advice: Turn on ufw (or another firewall) with rules for only the ports you mean to offer.
checks.title: Firewall
checks.why: Without a firewall every listening service is reachable from any network the server is on.

checks.advice: Bind services to 127.0.0.1 or the Tailscale address when only you need them.
checks.title: Services listening on every interface
checks.why: A service bound to every interface is reachable from every network the server is on, unless a firewall stops it.

checks.advice: Bind it to 127.0.0.1 (or a Docker network without published ports) and reach it over Tailscale or an SSH tunnel.
checks.title: Database or cache open to the network
checks.why: Databases and caches are often reachable without a password and are a common target.

checks.advice: Publish ports on 127.0.0.1 or the Tailscale address ("127.0.0.1:8080:80"), or filter in the DOCKER-USER chain.
checks.title: Docker ports bypass ufw
checks.why: Docker writes its own iptables rules ahead of ufw's, so a port Docker publishes on every interface is open even if ufw denies it.

checks.advice: With password logins on, install fail2ban (its sshd jail is on by default on Debian and Ubuntu) or turn passwords off.
checks.title: Brute-force protection
checks.why: fail2ban, CrowdSec or sshguard block addresses that keep failing to log in.

checks.advice: Install them from the Updates screen.
checks.title: Security updates waiting
checks.why: Known holes stay open until the fix is installed.

checks.advice: Install unattended-upgrades and turn it on with dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades.
checks.title: Automatic security updates
checks.why: unattended-upgrades installs security fixes without waiting for you.

checks.advice: Reboot when it suits you (Reboot… on the Overview).
checks.title: Reboot needed
checks.why: A new kernel or system library is not in use until the server restarts.

checks.advice: Check who created it; remove it or give it its own user id.
checks.title: Second root account
checks.why: Any account with user id 0 is root; an unexpected one is a classic sign of a break-in.

checks.advice: Lock it (sudo passwd -l <name>) or give it a password.
checks.title: Account with an empty password
checks.why: An account with an empty password can log in on the console, and over SSH wherever empty passwords are allowed.

checks.advice: Remove the -H tcp://… listener from the Docker daemon, or use 2376 with client certificates.
checks.title: Docker API on the network
checks.why: Port 2375 is Docker's API without TLS: anyone who reaches it controls the server as root.

checks.advice: Drop the setting unless the app needs it; tools such as Portainer, Watchtower and Traefik need the socket by design.
checks.title: Container with host access
checks.why: Privileged containers, host networking or PID, and the Docker socket or / mounted inside give a container root on the host.

checks.advice: Unlock Docker with sudo on the Docker screen, then check again.
checks.title: Containers not checked
checks.why: Docker would not list the containers for the ssh user.

checks.advice: Set kernel.randomize_va_space = 2 in /etc/sysctl.d/ (the default).
checks.title: Address space layout randomisation
checks.why: ASLR makes memory bugs much harder to exploit.

checks.advice: Turn on systemd-timesyncd or chrony (timedatectl set-ntp true).
checks.title: Clock synchronised
checks.why: Certificates, logs and two-factor codes depend on the right time.
